row.basis: Moses, fire, and not being consumed
row.note: Exodus makes the burning bush blaze without being consumed; it supplies the same Moses-and-fire encounter against which the commentary distinguishes Moses receiving guidance near fire from the wretched person entering fire in 87:12–13.

row.basis: Distant fire becoming a path
row.note: Moses turns aside to inspect the blazing bush, giving a narrative counterpart to the commentary's distant fire that draws him into a way of guidance.

row.basis: God's call from the bush
row.note: God calls Moses from the bush when he comes near; this is the fire-side encounter behind the commentary's sequence of fire, choice, and address.

row.basis: Moses chosen and sent against Pharaoh
row.note: At the bush God sends Moses to bring Israel from Egypt, a direct counterpart to the commentary's election at the fire and its later Pharaoh scene.

row.basis: Fire-side commission issuing in worship
row.note: God's sign to the commissioned Moses is that Israel will worship God at the mountain, supplying a biblical fire-to-worship movement beside the commentary's prayer after election.

row.basis: Q20:14 li-dhikri and Hebrew zikhri
row.note: At the bush the revealed name is God's perpetual memorial, Hebrew zikhri; its Semitic cognate relation to the commentary's li-dhikri joins divine name and remembrance at the same Moses encounter.

row.basis: Fire that leads by the way
row.note: The night pillar of fire gives Israel light in order to travel, a concrete biblical meeting of fire, path, and divine guidance rather than fire as punishment.

row.basis: Stephen's flame in the bush
row.note: Acts explicitly retells an angel appearing to Moses in a flame of a bush in the wilderness, preserving the scene around which the commentary gathers call and guidance.

row.basis: The bush appearance and Moses's sending
row.note: Stephen calls Moses the man sent by God as ruler and deliverer through the angel who appeared in the bush; it joins election at the fire to opposition from Egypt.

row.basis: The book of Moses at the bush
row.note: Jesus identifies the bush episode as a passage in the book of Moses, directly joining the commentary's final Moses pages to its opening fire encounter.

row.basis: Pharaoh's Egyptian sorcerers
row.note: Pharaoh summons wise men and sorcerers to meet Moses, the Torah's direct setting for the commentary's later gathering of Moses, Pharaoh, and magicians.

row.basis: Competing staffs and Aaron's victory
row.note: The magicians' staffs become serpents but Aaron's staff swallows them; this supplies the contest which the commentary reads through the magicians' eventual refusal of Pharaoh.

row.basis: Magicians acknowledge God's agency
row.note: When their art fails, the Egyptian magicians tell Pharaoh that the plague is God's finger; their recognition is a biblical counterpart to the commentary's magicians breaking with Pharaoh's claim.

row.basis: Egyptian magic publicly disgraced
row.note: Wisdom presents the Egyptian magic arts as shamed during the plague darkness, a Jewish expansion of the Moses-versus-magicians setting that makes magical competence fail before God's act.

row.basis: Jannes and Jambres oppose Moses
row.note: The letter gives traditional names to men who opposed Moses, a Christian reception of the Egyptian-magician conflict that the commentary brings into the Pharaoh scene.

row.basis: Refusal to worship under a king's fire threat
row.note: The Judeans refuse the king's gods even when a furnace is threatened; the scene closely meets the commentary's prostrating magicians who reject a tyrant's finite authority.

row.basis: Entrants into fire who are unharmed
row.note: The king sees the furnace's entrants walking unhurt; its outcome stands in deliberate tension with the commentary's person who enters the great fire and neither dies nor lives.

row.basis: A ruler's limited power over life
row.note: Jesus distinguishes people who can kill only the body from God who judges finally; this clarifies the commentary's assertion that Pharaoh rules only this worldly life while God is more enduring.

row.basis: Moses refuses Pharaoh's household
row.note: Moses refuses the status of Pharaoh's daughter's son, a specific Christian reading of the choice the commentary places beside Pharaoh's transient rule.

row.basis: Choosing suffering over passing pleasure
row.note: Moses chooses ill-treatment with God's people rather than sin's temporary enjoyment, closely matching the commentary's preference between the near worldly life and what lasts.

row.basis: Egyptian treasure weighed against a future reward
row.note: Moses values reproach above Egypt's treasures because he looks to recompense; the verse gives the commentary's choice and permanence an explicitly Mosaic Christian form.

row.basis: A tyrant ends present life, God raises to lasting life
row.note: A tortured brother tells the king that he may dismiss them from present life but the King of the world will raise them to everlasting life, closely meeting Pharaoh's threat and the better enduring life.

row.basis: Mortal death and resurrection unto life
row.note: Another brother contrasts death at human hands with hope of resurrection and tells the tyrant he has no resurrection to life; it is a pointed counter-formulation to neither dying nor living in the fire.

row.basis: A governor's brief fire and future judgment
row.note: Polycarp answers a ruler's fire threat by contrasting a short-lived flame with future judgment; the martyr tradition sharpens the commentary's contrast between Pharaoh's claimed lasting punishment and divine permanence.

row.basis: The Most High gives kingdoms to whom he wills
row.note: Daniel says the Most High rules human kingdoms and gives them as he chooses, directly contesting Pharaoh's self-exalting authority and joining highness to election.

row.basis: A humbled king praises the Most High
row.note: After his humiliation, the king blesses and honors the Most High whose dominion endures; it reverses the commentary's tyrannical high claim with praise and lasting rule.

row.basis: Undying worm and unquenched fire
row.note: Isaiah's final spectacle of the unquenched fire and worm that does not die is a close Hebrew-Bible horizon for the commentary's great fire and suspended death-life.

row.basis: Christian citation of undying worm and unquenched fire
row.note: Mark preserves Isaiah's image for Gehenna, making an explicit Christian counterpart to the commentary's fire in which ordinary death does not bring release.

row.basis: People seek death but death flees
row.note: In Revelation's torment people long to die yet cannot find death; this is a particularly close formulation beside the commentary's neither-dying-nor-living fire.

row.basis: Furnace as testing rather than annihilation
row.note: The furnace tests silver and gold while God tests hearts, supplying the corrective operation of fire that the commentary sets beside fire as punishment.

row.basis: Refining and purifying through fire
row.note: The divine messenger sits as a refiner and purifier of silver; this gives a biblical analogue for the commentary's distinction between a fire that sets something right and a fire endured as ruin.

row.basis: Dross removed so silver becomes usable
row.note: Removing dross from silver leaves material for the smith, a precise counterpart to the commentary's furnace foam: what is waste departs while what is useful remains.

row.basis: Gold tested in fire and the righteous in humiliation
row.note: Sirach's fire-testing of gold supplies a Jewish wisdom formulation for the commentary's corrective fire, without making it identical to the punitive fire.

row.basis: Fire tests the quality of each work
row.note: Paul's fire reveals whether work endures, directly extending the commentary's fire, useful remainder, and lasting good into a Christian assessment of works.

row.basis: Saved as through fire
row.note: Paul can describe a person whose work burns yet who is saved through fire; that different result makes a useful counterpoint to the commentary's condemned person inside the great fire.

row.basis: Waters apportioned by measure
row.note: Job says God established weight for wind and measured the waters, closely meeting the commentary's flood running in valleys according to measure.

row.basis: God measures the waters and creation
row.note: Isaiah pictures God measuring waters in his hand and the cosmos by span, expanding the commentary's measuring scene from floodwater to ordered creation.

row.basis: All things arranged by measure, number, and weight
row.note: This Jewish wisdom formula directly parallels the commentary's repeated movement from measured water to a created order apportioned by God.

row.basis: Rain makes earth sprout and yield
row.note: Rain descends, waters the earth, and makes it bear seed and bread; it is the biblical side of the commentary's rain, pasture, cultivated field, and beneficial yield.

row.basis: Rain makes grass sprout in waste ground
row.note: God's rain satisfies desolate ground and causes grass to spring up, a precise meeting of the commentary's rain-shaken earth and brought-forth pasture.

row.basis: God causes grass and cultivated vegetation to grow
row.note: The psalm distinguishes grass for animals and vegetation for human cultivation, furnishing a close biblical landscape for the commentary's pasture and worked soil.

row.basis: Fruitful tree by streams that does not wither
row.note: The water-planted tree bears fruit and does not wither, concretely supplies the commentary's useful, enduring side of water and vegetation.

row.basis: Chaff driven away
row.note: The wicked are wind-driven chaff, a biblical residue image beside the commentary's flood-carried foam and dried pasture that do not remain.

row.basis: Roaring waters and dispersed chaff
row.note: Nations roar like waters but flee like chaff before wind; this joins rushing flood imagery to transient residue as the commentary does.

row.basis: Floodwater washes away earth
row.note: Water wears stone and sweeps away soil, a literal counterpart to the commentary's flood carrying off what has dried and become refuse.

row.basis: Grass withers and flower fades
row.note: Isaiah's grass and flower wither under divine breath, giving a close biblical form to the commentary's worldly life becoming dried pasture.

row.basis: God's word stands forever after grass withers
row.note: The word's permanence is set directly against withering grass, completing the commentary's contrast between transient vegetation and what remains.

row.basis: All flesh as grass
row.note: First Peter reapplies the grass-and-fading-flower image to mortal human life, a Christian articulation of the commentary's worldly-life-as-grass scene.

row.basis: The word remains forever
row.note: The citation's next verse makes the Lord's word endure forever, matching the commentary's passage from drying life to an enduring word and future.

row.basis: Rain-drinking ground that yields a useful crop
row.note: Ground receives rain and produces a crop useful to its cultivators, a close Christian counterpart to the commentary's worked field that grows and remains beneficial.

row.basis: Thorny ground ending in burning
row.note: Ground producing thorns is rejected and ends in burning; it gives the commentary's neglected weed, field, and fire a sharply opposed agricultural outcome.

row.basis: Break fallow ground and do not sow among thorns
row.note: Jeremiah turns cultivation into moral exhortation, making a direct Jewish parallel for the commentary's ploughed field versus vegetation left to become waste.

row.basis: Sow righteousness and break fallow ground
row.note: Hosea links cultivated ground, righteousness, and a coming divine response, a close ethical field analogue to the commentary's falah-like salvation and lasting crop.

row.basis: Prepared vineyard yielding wild grapes
row.note: The carefully cultivated vineyard gives wild fruit instead of the expected crop; it adds a prophetic moral version of the commentary's contrast between worked land and uncontrolled growth.

row.basis: A harvested sheaf deliberately left for others
row.note: The forgotten sheaf must remain for the resident alien, orphan, and widow, concretely illuminating the commentary's claim that a field's produce has a due share left behind.

row.basis: Sowing for decay or eternal life
row.note: Sowing to flesh reaps corruption while sowing to Spirit reaps eternal life, translating the commentary's worldly and afterlife fields into a moral agricultural choice.

row.basis: Doing good and reaping in due season
row.note: The promise that persistent good will reap at the proper time supplies a Christian counterpart to the commentary's lasting good that remains after the transient growth goes.

row.basis: Wheat gathered and weeds burned
row.note: The parable preserves wheat while gathering weeds for burning, closely pairing the commentary's useful field, rejected vegetation, division, and fire.

row.basis: Unfruitful branch dries and is thrown into fire
row.note: A branch not abiding is dried, gathered, and burned, a concentrated Christian image for the commentary's dried vegetation and fire-bound outcome.

row.basis: Human body formed from earth
row.note: God forms the human from ground and breathes life into it, furnishing the body-and-earth side of the commentary's creating and fashioning pair.

row.basis: Skin, flesh, bones, and sinews fashioned
row.note: Job describes God clothing and knitting the body, a concrete biblical counterpart to the commentary's secondary sense of bodily and embryonic formation.

row.basis: Formed in the womb and appointed
row.note: Before forming Jeremiah in the womb God knows, consecrates, and appoints him; it joins formation, election, and a divine mission as the commentary does at Moses's fire.

row.basis: Maker from the womb who has chosen
row.note: Isaiah calls God the maker and former from the womb and names the chosen servant, an unusually close pairing for the commentary's crafted body and selection.

row.basis: A mortal shaped in a mother's womb
row.note: Wisdom describes ordinary human formation in the womb from earthly mortality, a Jewish literary counterpart to the commentary's womb-to-earth connection.

row.basis: The servant made a polished arrow
row.note: Isaiah's servant is made into a polished arrow and kept hidden; this supplies the crafted-arrow secondary sense which the commentary finds in the creation verb.

row.basis: Clay, potter, and work of God's hand
row.note: The potter-clay image gives the commentary's craft language a biblical body-and-maker analogy without reducing it to a lexical echo.

row.basis: Set apart from the womb and called
row.note: Paul describes being set apart from his mother's womb and called by grace, a Christian counterpart to formed life that is also chosen for a task.

row.basis: Potter's authority over clay vessels
row.note: Paul uses a potter making vessels for different purposes, joining divine fashioning to differentiated allotment in the way the commentary connects creation and choice.

row.basis: God guides the blind on an unknown path
row.note: God leads blind people on paths they do not know and turns darkness into light, a close biblical formulation for the commentary's measure-then-guidance and fire-path scene.

row.basis: God's just scales and weights
row.note: The proverb makes weights and measures God's work, supporting the commentary's secondary move from cosmic measuring to a just apportioned share.

row.basis: Cleansing from impurities and idols
row.note: God sprinkles clean water, cleanses Israel, and removes its idols, giving the commentary's purification and Abrahamic distance from idolatry a single biblical cleansing horizon.

row.basis: Proclaiming the divine name and ascribing greatness
row.note: Moses announces that he will proclaim YHWH's name and ascribe greatness to God, a close Torah counterpart to the commentary's praise of the exalted Lord and mention of the name.

row.basis: The exalted name alone praised
row.note: The psalm calls for praise of YHWH's name because that name alone is exalted above earth and heaven, closely meeting the commentary's name, praise, and highness.

row.basis: Abraham invokes El Elyon, God Most High
row.note: Abraham names YHWH El Elyon, God Most High; Hebrew elyon and the commentary's al-Ala share the highness root and join the title to Abraham named in 87:19.

row.basis: The high and lofty one revives the lowly
row.note: The high and lofty God dwells with the contrite in order to revive them, pairing the commentary's highness with its purified, responsive person rather than the arrogant ruler.

row.basis: Prayer that hallows God's name
row.note: The opening petition of the Lord's Prayer hallows the Father's name, an explicit Christian prayer counterpart to the commentary's remembering the Lord's name and praying.

row.basis: Secret things and revealed obligations
row.note: The secret belongs to God while what is revealed is for communal obedience, a precise Torah counterpart to the commentary's hidden divine matter and disclosed teaching.

row.basis: God knows and reveals hidden things
row.note: Daniel says God reveals deep and hidden things and knows what is in darkness, closely meeting the commentary's God who knows what is open and concealed.

row.basis: Do not forget the revelation and teach it
row.note: Israel must guard itself from forgetting what it saw and make it known to children, directly paralleling the commentary's word gathered, not forgotten, and offered as reminder.

row.basis: Write and teach the song as a witness
row.note: God tells Moses to write a song, teach it, and put it in Israel's mouths; it supplies a Mosaic written-and-remembered form for the commentary's recitation and warning.

row.basis: A song not forgotten from descendants' mouths
row.note: The divinely given song will not be forgotten from descendants, a particularly close biblical analogue to the commentary's not-forgetting and enduring instruction.

row.basis: Book in the mouth and continual meditation
row.note: Joshua is told not to let the Torah book depart from his mouth but to meditate on it day and night, matching the commentary's preserved speech, remembrance, and practice.

row.basis: Forgetting a word of study
row.note: The Mishnah applies Deuteronomy's warning to the deliberate forgetting of a learned word; it is a Jewish interpretive intensification of the commentary's not-forgetting motif.

row.basis: Not a forgetful hearer but a doer
row.note: James contrasts the forgetful hearer with the persevering doer of the perfect law, directly pairing the commentary's reminder with its division between response and avoidance.

row.basis: Life and good set against death and evil
row.note: Moses sets life and good before Israel against death and evil, a Torah form of the two human outcomes the commentary traces from reminder through fire and purification.

row.basis: Choose life
row.note: The call to choose life gives explicit Mosaic form to the commentary's language of preference and its contrast between the near life and what truly endures.

row.basis: Everlasting life and everlasting abhorrence
row.note: Daniel's awakening divides people between everlasting life and enduring disgrace, furnishing a biblical future horizon for the commentary's high ranks and great fire.

row.basis: This world as corridor before the world to come
row.note: Rabbi Jacob calls this world a vestibule before the world to come, a precise rabbinic frame for the commentary's worldly life versus the later, enduring life.

row.basis: Good deeds here and bliss in the world to come
row.note: The saying weighs repentance and good deeds in this world together with the incomparable bliss of the world to come, closely mapping the commentary's earthly choice and better permanence.

row.basis: Seen things temporary and unseen things eternal
row.note: Paul explicitly contrasts the temporary visible with the eternal unseen, giving the commentary's dunya-versus-lasting formulation a close Christian analogue.

row.basis: The world passes, the doer remains
row.note: The world and its desire pass away while the one doing God's will remains forever, directly matching the commentary's transient life and lasting good.

row.basis: Eternal punishment and eternal life
row.note: The final separation gives the two groups eternal punishment or eternal life, a Christian counterpart to the commentary's split between fire and the purified, praying person.

row.basis: The righteous beyond torment
row.note: The righteous are in God's hand and no torment touches them, providing a Jewish wisdom contrast to the commentary's person destined for the great fire.

row.basis: Furnace of torment opposed to a place of rest
row.note: The apocalyptic vision displays the furnace of Gehenna opposite a place of rest, a Jewish eschatological pairing for the commentary's fire and enduring differentiated outcome.

row.basis: Moses writes all the words of YHWH
row.note: Moses writes the divine words after Sinai, a direct Torah antecedent for the commentary's closing appeal to Moses's early pages.

row.basis: The written book of the covenant read aloud
row.note: Moses reads the book of the covenant to the people, bringing written pages together with recitation and hearing as in the commentary's preserved reminder.

row.basis: Moses completes writing Torah in a book
row.note: The verse explicitly depicts Moses finishing the words of Torah in a book, the clearest canonical textual counterpart to Moses's pages in 87:19.

row.basis: Rabbinic attribution of Moses's book
row.note: The Talmud's statement that Moses wrote his book is a Jewish reception of Mosaic textual authority relevant to the commentary's named pages of Moses.

row.basis: A restored corpus of revealed books
row.note: Ezra's scribes complete ninety-four books after the law's loss, a Jewish apocalyptic meditation on preserving and differentiating former sacred writings.

row.basis: Abraham keeps charge, commandments, statutes, and laws
row.note: Genesis attributes comprehensive obedience to Abraham, giving canonical footing for the commentary's Abrahamic former-scripture claim without assuming a canonical Abraham book.

row.basis: Abraham observed Torah before its giving
row.note: The Talmud reads Genesis 26:5 as Abraham's fulfillment of the whole Torah before Sinai, a major Jewish interpretation beside the commentary's Abrahamic pages.

row.basis: Jesus says Moses wrote of him
row.note: Jesus grounds his appeal in Moses's writing, a Christian interpretation of Mosaic pages that belongs beside the commentary's appeal to Moses as an earlier written authority.

row.basis: Scripture speaks beforehand to Abraham
row.note: Paul personifies Scripture as announcing blessing beforehand to Abraham, a Christian rereading that makes Abraham a recipient of prior scriptural proclamation.

row.basis: Abraham's ancestors serve other gods
row.note: Joshua locates Abraham's family beyond the river among worshippers of other gods, supplying canonical background for the commentary's Abrahamic plea to be kept from idols.

row.basis: God takes and leads Abraham
row.note: God takes Abraham from beyond the river and leads him through Canaan, matching the commentary's Abrahamic selection and its wider path-and-guidance movement.

row.basis: Put away foreign gods and serve YHWH
row.note: In the Abrahamic ancestral context Joshua calls Israel to remove foreign gods and serve YHWH, a direct biblical counterpart to the commentary's avoidance of idols.

row.basis: Choose whom you will serve
row.note: Joshua's demand to choose service of YHWH or other gods makes the commentary's preference theme concrete at the point of idolatry.

row.basis: Abraham's idol challenge and the furnace
row.note: The midrash has Abraham reject idols and be cast into Nimrod's furnace, a Jewish expansion that tightly joins the commentary's Abrahamic anti-idolatry with its repeated fire scenes.

row.basis: Abraham obeys a call into an unknown destination
row.note: Abraham obeys and goes out without knowing his destination, a Christian counterpart to the commentary's Abrahamic trust, calling, and path imagery.

row.basis: A voice heard from the middle of fire
row.note: Israel hears God's voice from fire but sees no form; this provides a wider Sinai form of the commentary's fire as a place of speech and revelation.

row.basis: The day and hour known only to the Father
row.note: Jesus says the decisive day and hour are known to the Father alone, a close Christian analogue to the commentary's divinely concealed hour.

row.basis: Times and seasons fixed by the Father's authority
row.note: Jesus withholds the times and seasons as the Father's own domain, complementing the commentary's hidden temporal decree without claiming the same formulation.

row.basis: A rite performed in remembrance
row.note: Jesus commands the meal to be done in his remembrance; its explicit liturgical remembering is a Christian parallel to the commentary's fire-side prayer for remembrance.

row.basis: Magic books surrendered and burned
row.note: Former practitioners publicly burn their magical books after confession, a later Christian scene of renouncing magic that complements the commentary's converted magicians without repeating its plot.

row.basis: A ruler aspiring to be like the Most High
row.note: The arrogant ruler seeks equality with the Most High, a non-Pharaoh biblical analogue for the commentary's additional Pharaoh claim to supreme height.

row.basis: Lake of fire called the second death
row.note: Revelation names the fiery lake the second death; its wording supplies a deliberate Christian contrast to the commentary's fire in which death and life are both denied.

row.basis: Faith tested as gold by fire
row.note: The letter compares tested faith to gold proved by fire, a Christian refinement image for the commentary's corrective fire and enduring value.

row.basis: The rich person fading like grass's flower
row.note: James uses scorched grass and fallen flower for the rich person's passing career, a specific Christian application of the commentary's worldly-life-as-drying-vegetation image.

row.basis: Restless waters casting up mud
row.note: The wicked are like a turbulent sea that throws up mire, a related prophetic water-and-waste image beside the commentary's flood-borne scum; the material correspondence is indirect.

row.basis: Following the light on the way to life
row.note: Jesus promises that followers of the world's light will not walk in darkness but have life's light; it is a Christian path-and-light counterpart to the commentary's fire sought for guidance.

row.basis: Cleansed bodies and drawing near in worship
row.note: The faithful draw near with hearts sprinkled clean and bodies washed, joining purification and worship as the commentary joins tazkiya, name-remembrance, and prayer.

row.basis: Grace given according to measure
row.note: Grace is given to each according to the measure of Christ's gift, a Christian individual-allotment image relevant to the commentary's move from measuring to portioning.

row.basis: A measure of faith allotted by God
row.note: God assigns each person a measure of faith, supplying another specific Christian use of divinely apportioned measure beside the commentary's qadar imagery.

row.basis: Moses read in synagogues every Sabbath
row.note: Acts describes Moses as publicly read in every city from ancient generations, a Christian witness to the continuing recitation of the Mosaic writings invoked by the commentary.

row.basis: The song of Moses as praise
row.note: The heavenly worshippers sing the song of Moses in praise of God's great works, a Christian liturgical meeting of Moses, praise, and enduring divine rule.

row.basis: Receiving an unshakable kingdom and offering worship
row.note: The community receives an unshakable kingdom and offers acceptable worship with awe, a Christian framing for the commentary's worship and permanence after transient life.

row.basis: Abraham and the priest of God Most High
row.note: Hebrews names Melchizedek priest of God Most High in his encounter with Abraham, a Christian reuse of the highness title alongside Abraham; it is a title-and-scene meeting rather than a shared story.

row.basis: Abraham named God's friend and chosen lineage
row.note: Isaiah calls Israel the offspring of Abraham God's friend and the chosen servant, supporting the commentary's pairing of Abraham, election, and earlier divine promise.

row.basis: Abraham's early confrontation with household idols
row.note: The opening idol episodes are commonly cited for Abraham's testing and rejection of Terah's idols and fire-associated separation; the exact internal sequence should be verified, but it is a specific expansion of the commentary's anti-idolatry Abraham.

row.ref: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Moses II.20–21
row.basis: The unconsumed bush in Christian typology
row.note: In the burning-bush interpretation commonly placed in these sections, Gregory reads the bush's non-consumption through later Christian typology; the section numbering should be checked, but it is a concrete reception of the fire detail central to the commentary.

row.basis: Divine self-identification at the bush
row.note: At the same fire God identifies himself by name before Moses's mission; it directly accompanies the source context of Q20:14, where prayer and remembrance follow God's self-declaration.

row.basis: Approaching fire as holy ground
row.note: Moses may not approach casually and must remove his sandals because the fire-side ground is holy, adding a concrete bodily response to the commentary's fire that becomes election and worship.

row.basis: Moses's staff for signs
row.note: Moses receives the staff with which he will perform signs, supplying the Torah's concrete bridge from the bush commission to the commentary's staff-and-magicians scene.

row.basis: Elijah's prayer to the God of Abraham at a fire contest
row.note: Elijah invokes the God of Abraham before the altar fire and asks that Israel know God and his servant; it joins fire, Abraham, divine name, and a public contest of allegiance.

row.basis: Fire consuming the offering
row.note: The fire of YHWH falls on Elijah's offering, furnishing a Hebrew-Bible fire scene whose purpose is revelation and correction rather than the destruction of a condemned person.

row.basis: People fall on their faces and confess God
row.note: After the fire the people prostrate themselves and confess YHWH as God, a close narrative meeting of fire, praise, and bowing with the commentary's magicians' prostration.

row.basis: Fire descends with divine glory
row.note: At the temple dedication fire descends and God's glory fills the house, a further biblical scene in which fire marks divine presence rather than entry into punitive fire.

row.basis: Bowing and praise after the fire
row.note: Seeing the fire and glory, Israel bows and gives thanks for God's enduring steadfast love; it closely combines the commentary's fire, praise, prostration, and permanence.

row.basis: Write a memorial in a book and rehearse it
row.note: God tells Moses to write the event as a memorial in a book and place it in Joshua's hearing, directly joining Mosaic pages with remembrance and spoken teaching.

row.basis: Moses commanded to write covenant words
row.note: Moses is told to write the covenant words, another explicit Torah source for the commentary's final appeal to earlier Mosaic pages.

row.basis: A written Torah copy read throughout life
row.note: The king must write a Torah copy and keep it for continual reading and fear of God, a precise model of page, remembrance, obedience, and durable instruction.

row.basis: The Torah book kept as witness
row.note: The written Torah is placed beside the ark as a witness, giving the commentary's named Mosaic pages a preserved and judicial function.

row.basis: Moses records the stages of the journey
row.note: Moses writes Israel's journey-stages at God's command, meeting the commentary's scrolls with its fire-and-path movement.

row.basis: Book of remembrance for those who fear and esteem the name
row.note: A book of remembrance is written for God-fearers who honor the divine name, tightly joining the commentary's reminder, fearer, name, and earlier pages.

row.basis: Words shut up and book sealed until the end
row.note: Daniel is told to close the words and seal the book until the time of the end, a direct biblical combination of hidden end-time knowledge and written pages.

row.basis: Many purified and refined, while the wicked do not understand
row.note: The end-time division has many made pure and refined while the wicked continue blindly; it closely meets the commentary's tazkiya, reminder, and divided response.

row.basis: Those guiding many to righteousness shine forever
row.note: The wise shine and those who turn many to righteousness shine like stars forever, a biblical counterpart to guidance, high degrees, and lasting reward.

row.basis: Write the vision so a reader may run
row.note: The vision is written plainly on tablets for a reader in motion, a specific meeting of the commentary's pages, public reminder, and path imagery.

row.basis: A vision for an appointed end that must be awaited
row.note: The vision has an appointed time and may seem slow but will come, a close prophetic analogue to the commentary's concealed decisive hour.

row.basis: Word as lamp for foot and light for path
row.note: The word gives a lamp and path-light, supplying a biblical verbal-light counterpart to the commentary's fire sought as guidance.

row.basis: Command as lamp and teaching as light on life's way
row.note: The commandment is a lamp, teaching a light, and reproofs a way of life; it joins reminder, guidance, and life in terms specific to the commentary's movement.

row.basis: Walking through darkness by God's lamp
row.note: Job recalls walking through darkness by God's shining lamp, a concrete light-and-way image alongside the commentary's fire sought for a guide.

row.basis: Prayer to the Father who sees in secret
row.note: Jesus places prayer in the hidden room before the Father who sees in secret, directly combining the commentary's prayer-for-remembrance with its hidden divine knowledge.

row.basis: Nothing hidden from God's sight
row.note: All creatures are exposed before the God to whom account is given, a direct Christian formulation for the commentary's God who knows what is open and concealed.

row.basis: Hidden things brought to light at judgment
row.note: God will disclose hidden things of darkness and heart-motives, giving a judgmental sequel to the commentary's hidden matter and differentiated outcomes.

row.basis: No one can hide beyond God's sight
row.note: The prophet asks whether anyone can hide in secret places from the God who fills heaven and earth, closely matching the commentary's claim of divine knowledge of the hidden.

row.basis: Hearing and doing words builds on rock
row.note: The person who hears Jesus's words and does them is likened to a wise builder, a Christian response-to-reminder counterpart to the commentary's beneficial admonition.

row.basis: Rain and floods fail to overthrow the founded house
row.note: Rain, flood, and wind strike the rock-founded house but it remains, directly meeting the commentary's flood and the contrast between what goes away and what remains.

row.basis: Hearing without doing builds on sand
row.note: The hearer who does not act on the words builds on sand, providing a counterpart to the commentary's person who avoids the reminder.

row.basis: Flood destroys the house with no foundation
row.note: Rain and floods bring a great fall to the sand-founded house, completing the commentary's water-borne testing and opposed human outcomes.

row.basis: Refined in the furnace of affliction
row.note: God refines Israel in an affliction-furnace, an explicit prophetic development of the commentary's fire as corrective work rather than only punishment.

row.basis: A remnant refined by fire and calling God's name
row.note: God brings a remnant through fire, refines it, and answers when it calls the divine name, closely coupling fire, purification, name, and responsive relationship.

row.basis: Fire consumes stubble because teaching is rejected
row.note: Fire devours stubble and dry grass because people reject God's teaching, a very close prophetic fusion of dried vegetation, fire, and refusal of reminder.

row.basis: God's word like fire
row.note: The divine word is likened to fire and a hammer, supporting the commentary's movement from recited reminder to a fire that actively corrects.

row.basis: God as consuming fire
row.note: Hebrews names God a consuming fire in a worship context, a concise Christian meeting of the commentary's divine fire, awe, and praise.

row.basis: Saving someone by snatching them from fire
row.note: Jude distinguishes rescuing people from fire from sharing their defilement, a concrete Christian complement to the commentary's concern with approaching versus entering fire.

row.basis: Wheat gathered and chaff burned with unquenchable fire
row.note: The coming judge stores wheat but burns chaff, tightly combining the commentary's useful remainder, agricultural waste, human division, and great fire.

row.basis: Fruit-bearing branches pruned for greater fruit
row.note: The grower prunes fruitful branches so they bear more fruit, supplying the corrective cultivation missing from the dried-and-burned branch image already developed by the commentary.

row.basis: Earth commanded to bring forth vegetation
row.note: Creation begins with the earth bringing forth seed-bearing vegetation and fruit trees, an immediate Torah counterpart to the commentary's Creator bringing forth pasture.

row.basis: Rain, field growth, and a worker for the ground
row.note: Before cultivated plants appear, the text notes both the absence of rain and of a human to work the soil, closely joining the commentary's rain, earth, body, and cultivated field.

row.basis: Seasonal rain producing land-yield and field fruit
row.note: God's rain gives land its yield and trees their fruit, a covenantal counterpart to the commentary's rain-fed field and lasting useful produce.

row.basis: Teaching falling like rain on grass
row.note: Moses compares teaching to rain, dew, and showers on tender grass, directly connecting the commentary's reminder to its water-and-pasture landscape.

row.basis: Growth like grass beside watercourses
row.note: The renewed descendants spring up among grass like trees by water, a close prophetic image for the commentary's watered growth instead of dried refuse.

row.basis: Earth and garden making righteousness and praise sprout
row.note: As earth makes sprouts grow, God makes righteousness and praise grow, joining the commentary's cultivated field to purification and praise.

row.basis: Created things wear out but salvation lasts forever
row.note: Heavens vanish, earth wears out, and inhabitants die, while God's salvation and righteousness endure; this closely matches the commentary's temporary worldly life and better permanence.

row.basis: Arabic mar'a and Hebrew mir'eh for pasture
row.note: Ezekiel depicts God feeding Israel in good pasture, Hebrew mir'eh, cognate with the commentary's Arabic mar'a; it turns the shared pasture image toward sustained divine shepherding.

row.basis: Arabic tazakka and Hebrew yizkeh around purity
row.note: Job asks how a human, including one born of woman, can be pure, using Hebrew yizkeh from the z-k-y root cognate with the commentary's tazakka; its setting adds bodily finitude to purification.

row.basis: Arabic hayat and Hebrew hayyim in the command to choose life
row.note: Beyond the existing choice motif, the Hebrew command choose hayyim and the commentary's hayat are cognate life terms; the verse grounds its life-choice in an explicit Semitic formulation.

row.basis: Praise offered with lips confessing God's name
row.note: The community continually offers praise to God as the fruit of lips acknowledging the name, a direct Christian liturgical counterpart to the commentary's name, praise, and prayer.

row.basis: Prayers ascending as a memorial before God
row.note: Cornelius's prayers and alms rise as a memorial before God, a specific Christian use of prayer and remembrance that complements the commentary's li-dhikri.

row.basis: Hope issuing in self-purification
row.note: Those who hold the eschatological hope purify themselves, a compact Christian parallel to the commentary's purified person oriented toward the enduring future.

row.basis: Draw near, cleanse hands, and purify hearts
row.note: James pairs drawing near to God with cleansing and a divided heart's purification, directly meeting the commentary's tazkiya and worshipful response.

row.basis: Holy ones of the Most High possess an everlasting kingdom
row.note: The holy ones of the Most High receive and possess the kingdom forever, a direct biblical meeting of highestness, elevated status, and permanence.

row.basis: Everlasting kingdom given to the people of the Most High
row.note: All dominions serve the holy people whose kingdom endures, answering the commentary's tyrant's temporary rule with lasting high rule under God.

row.basis: A ruler claims divinity and is answered that he is mortal
row.note: The ruler of Tyre claims to sit as a god but is told he is human, a close prophetic counter-scene for the commentary's Pharaoh claiming supreme status.

row.basis: Hearing the word passes from death into life
row.note: The one who hears and believes has eternal life and has crossed from death to life, a Christian response-to-reminder counterpart to the commentary's fire-bound non-life and purified alternative.

row.basis: Present goods reversed into future comfort and anguish
row.note: Abraham contrasts the rich man's received good things in life with his later anguish and Lazarus's comfort, closely framing the commentary's worldly preference and later permanence.

row.basis: Broad way leading to destruction
row.note: The broad gate and way end in destruction, providing a Christian path-and-outcome counterpart to the commentary's guidance, choice, and fire.

row.basis: Narrow way leading to life
row.note: The difficult way leads to life and few find it, sharpening the commentary's sought guidance and its contrast between life-oriented response and loss.

row.basis: Future with death abolished
row.note: Revelation's renewed world abolishes death, mourning, and pain; its eschatological endpoint gives a Christian counter-horizon to the commentary's fire where neither death nor life occurs.

row.basis: Righteous enjoying divine radiance in the world to come
row.note: The Talmud's world-to-come scene gives the righteous crowns and enjoyment of divine radiance, a Jewish interpretive counterpart to enduring high degrees rather than temporary worldly life.

row.basis: God reveals a secret to prophetic servants
row.note: Amos says God discloses the divine secret to prophets, a specific prophetic counterpart to the commentary's hidden matter becoming disclosed guidance.

row.basis: Melchizedek as priest of God Most High blessing Abraham
row.note: The priestly blessing names God Most High in an Abraham scene, supplying the canonical context for the highness title already central to the commentary's first and last images.

row.basis: A name highly exalted above every name
row.note: God highly exalts a name above every name, a Christian reapplication of name-and-highness that is relevant to the commentary's praise of the highest Lord but does not share its speaker.

row.basis: Every knee bends at the exalted name
row.note: The universal bending of knees at the name gives a Christian liturgical analogue to the commentary's prostration and exalted name, with a different christological setting.

row.basis: Green marsh plant withering before other growth
row.note: A water-dependent plant withers while still green, a specific wisdom image for the commentary's pasture turning into waste; the water setting differs from its valley flood.

row.basis: Floodwaters sweep away a false refuge
row.note: Hail and overflowing waters expose a refuge made of falsehood, a prophetic water judgment that complements the commentary's flood separating what vanishes from what remains.

row.basis: Weeds gathered and burned at the age's end
row.note: Jesus explains the weed-and-fire image as an end-time sorting, a necessary interpretive continuation of the field scene and the commentary's future fire.

row.basis: Righteous shining in their Father's kingdom
row.note: The righteous shine in the kingdom after the furnace judgment, a Christian continuation that meets the commentary's high degrees and lasting reward.

row.basis: Abraham chosen to command his household in righteousness
row.note: God says Abraham is known so that he will direct his household in God's way of righteousness and justice, adding a canonical Abrahamic election-and-teaching counterpart to the former-pages claim.

row.basis: Abraham's early rejection of idolatry
row.note: These verses are commonly associated with young Abram's recognition of the earth's error in following carved images and his prayer for deliverance; exact wording and division should be verified, but the link is a specific Jewish precursor to the commentary's anti-idolatry Abraham.
